issues.issue: The clause says the Agreement "shall be effective as hereinafter provided", while Section 17 makes it "effective as of the date first above written"; the deferred-effectiveness promise is never separately supplied. The gap is small but a court could be asked when the instrument took effect.

A payment obligation is placed in a WHEREAS recital rather than in the operative text, raising the recital-versus-operative question of whether the $2,000 initial location fee is a promise or mere background. Section 3(B)(2) states the parallel subsequent-well fee operatively, sharpening the contrast.

This recital says Farmee "may acquire an interest in the Farmout Lands described in Exhibit A and Exhibit B", while the operative Section 2(D) limits what can ever be acquired to operating rights in 80-acre and 40-acre circles around producing wells. The recital thus promises more than the operative earning provisions deliver.

Section 1 describes Exhibit "C" as a "Geological Requirement Letter", but the attached Exhibit C is a schedule headed "GEOLOGICAL REQUIREMENTS" and no letter exists. The mismatch is minor but concerns what document is incorporated.

The definition makes a dry hole that is "plugged and abandoned" a "completed well", so the same term covers both a producer and a failure. A court could be asked which sense governs where the operative text speaks of a "completed" well.

The defined term "completed well" is not the phrase the operative provisions use; Sections 3(D) and 3(B) instead speak of a well "completed as a well capable of production in paying quantities". The relationship between the defined term and that operative formula is left unresolved.

"Earning well" is defined but appears nowhere in the operative text, which instead uses "farmout well" and "well capable of production in paying quantities". An unused definition invites argument about which wells it was meant to capture.

Rights turn on whether a well is "capable of producing in paying quantities", a phrase left undefined and notoriously contestable, and the 80/40-acre "circle" is described by area without any stated radius or survey method. Both are terms whose boundary a court would have to fix.

The Exhibit "D" form of assignment leaves the acreage of the circle blank, so the instrument that actually conveys the rights does not carry forward the 80/40-acre measure fixed here. The two must be reconciled to know what is conveyed.

"Lease burdens" ends with the catch-all "and other similar burdens on production" after an enumeration of royalty, overriding royalty and production payment, leaving its reach open to an ejusdem generis argument. Whether items such as net profits interests fall inside is unresolved.

The defined term "lease burdens" is never used anywhere in the operative sections or exhibits, so nothing in the instrument tells a court what work the definition does. Its relationship to Section 4's reserved overriding royalty is left unstated.

The definition turns on capability of producing in "commercial quantities", a term used nowhere else and undefined, while the rest of the Agreement measures wells by "paying quantities". Which standard applies to a shut-in well is open.

This definition requires that the well "has previously produced", but Section 7(A) imposes the shut-in royalty on any capable well "whether or not such well has already produced". The two cannot both describe the class of shut-in wells.

A "subsequent well" is defined as one drilled after "the drilling and completion" of the test well, yet Section 3(B) allows subsequent wells where the test well was merely "plugged and abandoned". Whether a dry test hole satisfies the definition's completion requirement is unresolved.

"Payout" compares "gross proceeds attributable to the sale or production from a well" to "the cost of drilling, completing and equipping" it, without saying whose costs, whether operating costs count, or what "proceeds attributable to ... production" (as opposed to sale) means. Each of those is a live construction question.

The test well may be sited off the Farmout Lands on "a drilling unit that includes all or a portion of Farmout Lands", but Section 2(D) measures Operating Rights Earned by a circle around the well limited to "that portion and only that portion of the Farmout Lands". What is earned by an off-premises unit well is left unclear.

This subsection requires only that Farmee "commence the actual drilling" by August 31, 1996, whereas Section 16 conditions the Right of First Refusal on Farmee having "drill[ed] and complete[d] the test well on or before August 31, 1996". The two dates cannot both be met on the schedule Section 3(A)(3) allows.

The deadline is stated as a fragment with no verb — it fixes a period but never says what must occur within it or by whom. Whether "completion" means the Section 2(A) "completed well" standard has to be supplied by construction.

This subsection makes subsequent drilling an "option" of Farmee, but Section 3(B)(3) says Farmee "must commence the actual drilling of two (2) Subsequent Wells" by December 31, 1996, and Section 13(A) treats failure under 3(B)(3) as a terminating breach of "drilling commitments". Whether subsequent wells are optional or obligatory is squarely in issue.

The continuous-development sentence is self-contradictory on its face: "at Farmee's further option, it shall continuously develop the Farmout Lands by commencing ... a minimum of two (2) Subsequent Wells per calendar year" makes the same act simultaneously optional and mandatory. "Fully developed" is also left without any measure.

Section 13(A) treats this subsection as a source of automatic termination "as a consequence of Farmee's failure to meet the drilling commitments", yet 3(B)(3) contains no termination language and casts continuous development as Farmee's option. The two provisions cannot both be right about whether annual drilling is a commitment.

The trigger — a well "lost for any reason" or a "mechanical difficulty or formation or condition which would render further drilling impractical or impossible" — turns on the vague and largely self-judged word "impractical". Its boundary would have to be fixed by a court.

Delivery of the assignment is due only "within sixty (60) days after Farmor is satisfied that Farmee has complied with all its obligations", making the trigger Farmor's own subjective satisfaction with no standard, deadline or reasonableness qualifier. A court would have to decide whether that satisfaction may be withheld at will.

Forfeiture runs from sixty days after a well "has been completed as a well capable of production in paying quantities", but nothing fixes when that state is reached or who determines it. The date on which the forfeiture clock starts is therefore indeterminate.

Section 3(D)(1) makes Farmor's delivery obligation depend on Farmor's satisfaction after receiving Farmee's request, while this subsection forfeits the right if the request is late; the two clocks are measured from different, unsynchronised events. Reconciling the request deadline with the satisfaction condition requires construction.

This subsection measures earned depths by footage (surface to 100' below total depth, capped at 4,000'), while the Exhibit "D" assignment reserves everything "below the ____ formation" — a stratigraphic limit, with the formation left blank. The two measures of the vertical grant do not match.

The provision runs two inconsistent regimes together: drilling failures terminate the Agreement automatically, while defaults "other than above" terminate only after thirty days' notice and a failure to cure. Which side of that line a given breach falls on is left to argument.

Section 3(F) terminates the whole Agreement on a drilling default, whereas Section 5(B) terminates it only "as to the Unearned Farmout Lands" for wrongful abandonment, and Section 13(A) lumps both together as terminating the Agreement. The scope of termination cannot be settled from any one of them.

The royalty is on "gross proceeds received from the sale of oil and/or gas produced from wells drilled hereunder without deductions of any kind", which does not say at what point of sale proceeds are measured or whether post-production costs may be borne by the royalty. "Gross proceeds ... without deductions" is exactly the phrase such disputes turn on.

Section 4(A) allows "no deductions of any kind", but the Exhibit "D" assignment form reserves the same royalty "without deductions of any kind, except that Assignor shall bear its proportionate part of any severance tax". The instrument that implements the reservation contradicts the reservation itself.

The notice duty is triggered when a well is not capable of producing in paying quantities or "ceases production", a phrase with no duration or materiality qualifier, so any temporary interruption may trip it. Whether a brief cessation counts is a construction question.

Section 5(A) requires notice and abandonment when a well "ceases production", while Section 7(A) contemplates a capable well simply being shut in for 45 days or longer against a shut-in royalty. The same well can fall under both regimes with opposite consequences.

Termination follows if Farmee fails to give Farmor "a reasonable opportunity to consider its options", a standard stated without any measure even though Section 5(A) already prescribes exact 30-day and 48-hour windows. What more "reasonable opportunity" requires is undefined.

This subsection terminates the Agreement only "as to the Unearned Farmout Lands", yet Section 13(A) lists 5(B) among the provisions by which "This Farmout Agreement terminates". The scope of a 5(B) termination is inconsistent between the two.

The clause requires Farmee to assign "any Operating Rights Earned by Farmor and earned by Farmee", a garbled formula that attributes the same earned rights to both parties. Reimbursement at "estimated salvage value ... less estimated plugging costs" also leaves unsaid who makes the estimates.

Section 6 by its terms governs only a takeover "under the terms and conditions of Section 5", but Section 3(F) invokes Section 6 for a takeover on default of wells that have not satisfied the earning requirements. The default takeover has no complete mechanic of its own.

The clause charges a shut-in royalty "per well per year, prorated on a monthly basis" yet makes it "due and payable by the last day of each month any such well is shut-in", leaving annual versus monthly accrual unclear. The trigger "shut in for any reason" is also unqualified.

Section 7(A) applies to any capable well "whether or not such well has already produced", while Section 2(H) defines a "shut-in well" as one "that has previously produced and is still capable of producing in commercial quantities". The class of wells owing shut-in royalty differs between the two.
The notice duty is qualified by "When possible", a self-judging condition that supplies no test for when advance notice may be omitted. The obligation is effectively unmeasurable as drafted.

The indemnity covers losses "of any kind or character incurred by Farmor and arising out of, in connection with, or resulting from the operations, actions or omissions of Farmee" without saying whether it reaches losses caused by Farmor's own negligence. The bracketed enumeration also sits against the words "including but not limited to", leaving the catch-all's reach open.

Farmee must keep the Farmout Lands "free and clear from all liens", yet the Exhibit "D" assignment gives Assignor "a lien on all future production and proceeds" for unpaid overriding royalty and Section 15(D) contemplates liens created with Farmor's consent. The absolute prohibition cannot be read literally against those provisions.

"Farmor does not warrant title, either express or implied" is grammatically incoherent — the adjectives modify nothing — and the sentence never says whether statutory or after-acquired-title warranties are also disclaimed. A court would have to supply the intended disclaimer.

The clause says notices "shall be given as follows" and then supplies only addresses, phone and fax numbers, without specifying an acceptable method of delivery or when notice is deemed received. Whether a fax or telephone call is effective notice is left open.

Farmee must "acquire and/or maintain" three named kinds of insurance with no stated policy limits, deductibles or duration. Whether any particular level of coverage satisfies the covenant cannot be determined from the words.

The section is headed "MODIFICATIONS AND AMENDMENTS" but contains no amendment procedure at all; it is an after-acquired-interest clause, and its reach — "any subsequently acquired interest in such lands ... whether obtained directly or indirectly" — is stated without limit. The mismatch between heading and text is itself a construction problem.

The clause fixes the term by reference to two events only, without any outside date, so if neither occurs the Agreement runs indefinitely. Whether "until such time as" creates a perpetual instrument is open.

Section 13(A) says the Agreement "terminates pursuant to Sections 3(A)(2), 3(B)(3), 3(F), and/or 5(B)", but 3(A)(2) and 3(B)(3) are bare deadlines containing no termination language and 5(B) terminates only as to Unearned Farmout Lands; 13(B) also assumes "all Farmout Lands" can be earned though Section 2(D) permits earning only 80/40-acre circles. The term provision cannot be squared with the sections it cites.

Farmee must comply with all obligations, burdens and requirements "set forth hereunder or otherwise associated with the lands covered hereby", and the trailing catch-all has no stated source or boundary. What obligations are "otherwise associated with the lands" is entirely undefined.

Farmee must "settle surface damages" and restore the premises "as nearly as possible to its original condition", neither of which supplies a measurable standard or a baseline condition. How near is "as nearly as possible" would have to be construed.

Section 15(D) bars any assignment or encumbrance by Farmee without Farmor's prior written consent, while the Exhibit "D" assignment form expressly permits Assignee to assign down to a 25% working interest on mere written notice, requiring consent only for assignment of operator rights. The two assignment regimes conflict.

The right is labelled a "Right of First Refusal" but operates as a fixed-terms option — Farmor must offer before granting any farmout and Farmee accepts on preset terms — with no matching of any third-party offer. "One time" right and the fifteen-day election period compound the uncertainty about what triggers the offer duty.

The condition that Farmee "drills and completes the test well on or before August 31, 1996" is impossible to reconcile with Section 3(A)(2), which requires only that drilling commence by that date, and Section 3(A)(3), which allows 45 days after total depth to complete. The trigger for the right cannot be satisfied on the schedule the Agreement itself sets.

The statement that the terms "shall run with said Farmout Lands" asserts a real covenant without identifying the burdened estate or any privity, leaving open whether it binds successors in title as opposed to contracting parties. That is a classic point of construction in oil and gas instruments.

This clause makes the Agreement binding on "successors and assigns", while Section 15(D) provides the Agreement "may not be assigned, sublet, mortgaged, pledged, encumbered" by Farmee without Farmor's prior written consent. Whether assigns can exist at all has to be reconciled between the two.

The Agreement takes effect "as of the date first above written", yet the date lines on Exhibits A, C and D — all incorporated as part of the Agreement by Section 1 — are left blank. Which date governs the incorporated documents is unstated.

The schedule contains internal errors that affect what land is included: tract 228594F (5-1120) is listed twice at 3.65 and 391.60 acres, 228630F (5-1154) twice at .35 and 188.84, 228577F twice, and one entry "(5-1152) 10.12" carries no lease number. The described Farmout Lands cannot be determined with certainty from the list.

The tract schedule must be reconciled with the cover-page description of "5,400 acres, more or less" and with the Exhibit "B" plat, which Section 1 also makes part of the Agreement. A discrepancy between the written schedule and the plat would have to be resolved.

Exhibit C imposes every duty on "Operator", a term the Agreement never defines and never equates with Farmee, although Section 3(D) makes compliance with Exhibit C a condition of earning. Who owes these obligations if Farmee is not the operator is unresolved.

The paragraph requires a "qualified wellsite geologist" to "thoroughly and timely" examine samples and that cores be "properly and timely analyzed", none of which is given a measure. It also grants access to "EREX", an abbreviation used nowhere else in the instrument.

The obligation applies to "significant indications of reservoir quality porosity with hydrocarbon shows" and requires that they be "adequately tested in accordance with good oilfield practices", stacking three undefined standards on one another. Neither significance nor adequacy has any benchmark in the instrument.

The requirement of a "Routine daily prepaid report" appears to be a mechanical error for "prepared", and as written it imposes an unintelligible prepayment condition on the reporting duty. The sentence is also left unpunctuated at its end.

The duty attaches to "Non-routine occurrences such as notification of significant shows, intent to core, test or log", an open illustrative list whose outer boundary is undefined. Whether an occurrence outside the examples must be telephoned immediately is left to argument.

The list of required well surveys is a checkbox schedule whose marks are indeterminate — stray characters appear against Density and Neutron and the "Other" line is blank — so which surveys must actually be run cannot be read off the page. The obligation is left incomplete on its face.

"Timely notice of intent to core, test or log" fixes no period, and the only measure offered is the purpose clause that Farmor's representative "may be present to witness same". How much notice is enough is undetermined.

The lead-in requires "one copy" of the listed items, item (a) requires "Two final prints", and a free-standing heading "THREE COPIES:" precedes items (b) to (e); the number of copies actually owed is internally inconsistent. Item (e), "any other data pertinent", is also an unbounded catch-all.

Operator must furnish "full information on the completion progress, including one copy of the data listed below", so the enumerated items are illustrative of an undefined larger duty. What "full information" beyond the list requires is left open.

Exhibit C directs all reports to a different street address and a different addressee (Mike Stamper, 1989 E. Stone Drive) than Section 10(B) prescribes for notices to Farmor (Two Executive Park Place, Attn: Lester Zitkus). Which address governs well data notices requires reading the two together.

The granting clause depends entirely on blanks — the well number and the size of the "____ acre circle" are never filled in — so the form as incorporated conveys nothing identifiable. The description also refers to an "Exhibit A attached hereto" that does not exist in the form.

Section 2(D) fixes the earned area at an 80-acre circle for gas wells and a 40-acre circle for oil wells, but the assignment form that Section 3(D)(1) says shall be used leaves the acreage open. What is actually conveyed must be reconciled with Section 2(D).

The assignment endures "so long as oil and gas or either of them is produced in paying quantities" or the well is shut in, with no temporary-cessation savings period and no definition of paying quantities. When the assignment ends is precisely the kind of habendum question courts construe.

This habendum keeps the assignment alive while the well is shut in, but Section 5(A) requires Farmee to give notice and plug and abandon a well that "ceases production" or is not capable of paying production, and Section 7(A) conditions shut-in status on payment of a shut-in royalty. The three provisions give different answers for a non-producing well.

The Assignor conveys rights "necessary or convenient" for operations under the underlying deeds or leases, and "convenient" has no ascertainable limit. The scope of the easements and rights of way passing under the clause is therefore open.

The reserved royalty rate and the substance produced are both left blank ("equal to ____ ( __% of 8/8) ... from the sale of ____"), so the form cannot itself fix the reservation. The blanks go to the essential term of the reservation.

This clause reserves the royalty "without deductions of any kind, except that Assignor shall bear its proportionate part of any severance tax", while Section 4(A) of the Farmout Agreement reserves the same royalty "without deductions of any kind" with no exception. The severance-tax carve-out contradicts the governing reservation.

The clause reserves title to "the aforementioned lands, and all rights connected thereto" and then grants "other such rights" — a self-cancelling formula in which the reservation appears to swallow the grant. What was actually conveyed depends on construing that sentence.

The provision limits assignments that would reduce Assignee's "rights and interest in and to Well No. ___" below a "twenty-five percent (25%) working interest", although the instrument conveys operating rights rather than a working interest and never defines the latter. How the 25% floor is measured is unclear.

This clause permits assignments on written notice so long as a 25% interest is retained, whereas Section 15(D) of the Farmout Agreement forbids any assignment or encumbrance by Farmee without Farmor's prior written consent. The two consent regimes cannot both govern a transfer of the earned rights.

The reservation of "all strata and formations extending below the ____ formation" leaves the controlling formation blank, so the vertical limit of the assignment is undetermined on the face of the instrument. Nothing in the clause supplies a default.

The reservation is expressed stratigraphically while Section 3(E) of the Farmout Agreement measures the depths earned in footage — surface to 100' below total depth, capped at 4,000'. The two measures of the vertical severance do not correspond.

Binding the assignment on "successors and assigns" sits against Section 15(D) of the Farmout Agreement, which bars assignment by Farmee without Farmor's prior written consent. Whether assigns can take free of that restriction requires reading the two together.

Making the assignment "subject to the terms and conditions" of the Farmout Agreement is hard to square with Section 3(F), under which termination of the Agreement leaves Operating Rights Earned intact, and with Section 4's statement that the reserved override survives termination. Whether termination of the Farmout Agreement pulls down the assignment is left open.
